newsitem.title: UK: UK bank lending falls s/a 512 mln stg in Dec.
newsitem.headline: UK bank lending falls s/a 512 mln stg in Dec.

text.p: Total sterling lending by major British banking groups to the UK private sector fell by a seasonally adjusted 512 million stg in December, the British Bankers' Association (BBA) said.
This compares with a sharp rise of 4.255 billion stg in November and a six-monthly average increase of 2.860 billion.
"The fall in lending in December, of which 460 million stg was the result of a deline in repo claims, was accentuated by a securitisation to the value of around 300 million stg," the BBA said.
Consumer credit was up 443 million stg in December.
This compared with a November figure of 377 million stg and was close to the six-monthly average of 425 million.
Mortgage lending rose by 552 million stg compared with 606 million in November and a six-monthly average of 571 million.
Lending to the manufacturing sector was up 258 million stg while lending to the financial sector fell by 426 million stg following a sharp rise in November.
On the liabilities side, deposits from the private sector showed a fall of 357 million.
BBA director-general Tim Sweeney said that while December was otherwise a depressed month for the major banks' lending, personal sector credit demand held up fairly well.

"Overall, however, the banks' lending declined in December, with both industrial and commercial companies and the financial sector repaying funds over the month," he added. "A notable feature was a significant reduction in repo business."
In 1996 as a whole, mortgage lending rose five percent, virtually the same increase as in 1995, while consumer credit increased by close to 14 percent compared with 10 percent in 1995.

"In absolute terms, the increase in consumer credit was almost 50 percent higher than that recorded in 1995," Sweeney said. "Lending to industry and commerce rose by around five percent, slightly more than in the previous year."
